{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01FhWarUCm1cB3RFqX3zmFQM","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Worked examples: dependencies, validation gates, labels, reversibility, budgets, exceptions\n2\t\n3\tExamples for the rules in `SKILL.md`. This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\n4\tsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n5\t\n6\t## 1. Dependency kinds\n7\t\n8\t| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n9\t|---|---|---|---|\n10\t| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n11\t| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n12\t| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n13\t| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n14\t| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n15\t| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n16\t| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n17\t\n18\tCommon misses:\n19\t\n20\t- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n21\t- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n22\t  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n23\t- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n24\t- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n25\t\n26\t## 2. Validation gates\n27\t\n28\tFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n29\t\n30\t| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n31\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n32\t| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n33\t| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n34\t| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n35\t| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n36\t| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n37\t\n38\tShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\n39\tso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n40\t\n41\tA good acceptance threshold:\n42\t\n43\t- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n44\t  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n45\t  security, or legal judgment;\n46\t- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n47\t- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n48\t- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n49\t\n50\tAnti-patterns:\n51\t\n52\t- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n53\t  correct, or affordable enough.\n54\t- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n55\t  UNKNOWN has no number.\n56\t- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n57\t  sublayer.\n58\t- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n59\t- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n60\t  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n61\t\n62\t## 3. Reversibility\n63\t\n64\t| Tier | Examples |\n65\t|---|---|\n66\t| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n67\t| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n68\t| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n69\t\n70\tCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\n71\tbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\n72\tundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\n73\tirreversible operation.\n74\t\n75\tBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\n76\tprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n77\t\n78\tSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\n79\tinterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\n80\traw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\n81\tthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\n82\ton every row from day one.\n83\t\n84\t## 4. Budgets\n85\t\n86\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n87\t|---|---|---|---|\n88\t| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n89\t| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n90\t| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n91\t| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n92\t| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n93\t\n94\tRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\n95\tis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n96\t\n97\t## 5. Methodology exceptions\n98\t\n99\t| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n100\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n101\t| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n102\t| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n103\t| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n104\t| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n105\t\n106\tNot exceptions:\n107\t\n108\t- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n109\t- Brownfield work. Example of the normal method: a CI/CD platform for 50 services takes one real\n110\t  service through the new platform to production in Phase 0, with its old pipeline kept as the\n111\t  fallback, and migrates the rest in waves.\n112\t- Reading principle 6 for software you do not operate: a CLI's skeleton is the released package,\n113\t  installed the way users install it, renaming a real folder in dry-run mode (writes run on a\n114\t  disposable copy until the undo journal's gate passes).\n115\t- Data-protection regimes (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). They add risk/security and organizational\n116\t  dependencies, such as a business associate agreement before patient data reaches a new\n117\t  vendor, and the skeleton still runs in production on a designated test record.\n118\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"415a5311-1619-42a1-abca-8db7344031d5","uuid":"44d9d20d-8895-4145-9480-cf28707dd21d","timestamp":"2026-10-03T00:08:27.367Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\\Users\\nrvhari\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\dfa-eval\\2026-10-03-pilot-core\\plugins\\p140aff59\\skills\\dependency-first-architect\\reference\\validation.md","content":"# Worked examples: dependencies, validation gates, labels, reversibility, budgets, exceptions\n\nExamples for the rules in `SKILL.md`. {"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_lu6t6q72l2rd5ug6ydc27ki4bz2almpbkqcbywflmpcio7ixxpca","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# BUILD PLAN: Moving the patient scheduling system from on-premises to the cloud with no downtime\n\n**Assumptions this plan rests on.** Each one says what changes if it is false.\n- **(a) The app has a server tier.** I assume it is a web or app-server app on one relational database (SQL Server assumed) that only the hospital runs. If instead desktop clients connect straight to the database, moving users in groups first (Phase 2) means moving Citrix/VDI hosts instead, or skipping straight to the flip in Tradeoff 4.\n- **(b) HL7 messaging stays as it is.** HL7 v2 messages go through an on-premises interface engine to an on-premises EHR, and both stay where they are.\n- **(c) A cloud provider is chosen.** The hospital's enterprise agreement already names a provider that will sign a BAA. If no provider is chosen, that choice becomes an R3 gate in front of Phase 0.\n- **(d) \"No downtime\" allows a short write pause.** It means reads never stop and writes may pause for a few seconds at the database switch while clients retry. If even that is not allowed, Tradeoff 2 reopens. That would mean two databases both taking writes, which risks double-booking.\n\n## 1. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** move a live, PHI-bearing (HIPAA-protected patient data) scheduling application and its database from on-premises to a cloud provider. Schedulers, the call center, clinics, the patient portal and HL7 interfaces keep working throughout.\n- **Type:** infrastructure plus software. Brownfield. Not a small build: it holds regulated data, has R3 decisions and many teams.\n- **Dominant constraint:** availability, with correctness close behind.\n- **Worst failure:** two databases both accepting writes at the switch, or replication losing writes. Either loses, duplicates or double-books appointments, and patients miss care or show up to conflicting slots. PHI exposure in the cloud comes second; V2 guards it.\n\n**Inherited constraints** (this move does not change them; each line gives the cost to change):\n- **Single application:** the app stays one unit, not split into services. Changing that is a re-architecture project.\n- **Database engine and schema:** both stay. A different engine means a schema port and re-certification.\n- **HL7 v2:** messages still go through the existing interface engine. Changing that means re-testing every interface with the EHR and outside vendors.\n- **Staff logins:** they stay on the existing Active Directory / SSO. Changing that is a new trust boundary for all staff.\n- **EHR:** it stays on-premises.\n- **Downtime procedures:** the hospital's existing paper/business-continuity procedures stay the last-resort fallback.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Planned downtime | None. Reads stay up at all times. | REQUIREMENT (stated in the request) | V6, Phase 3 |\n| Write pause at the database switch | ≤ 60 s, with clients retrying | ASSUMPTION: proposed. The Director of Patient Access and the CMIO must confirm it as a REQUIREMENT before Phase 3. | V6 |\n| Latency (search a slot → book → confirm) | p95 ≤ the on-premises figure + 10% after the move | Measured value: BASELINE (Phase 0). Allowance: ASSUMPTION, to be confirmed with Patient Access. | V0 records it; V4, V5 |\n| Throughput | 2× the peak measured on-premises (booking surge on Monday mornings) | Peak: BASELINE (Phase 0). Headroom: ASSUMPTION. | V5 |\n| Availability (SLO) | ≥ the on-premises figure | BASELINE: UNKNOWN until Phase 0 measures it. IT Operations supplies it. | V7 |\n| RPO / RTO inside the cloud region | RPO 0 for committed bookings; writes resume ≤ 60 s after a zone failure | ASSUMPTION: synchronous copies across availability zones | V5 |\n| Disaster-recovery RPO / RTO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the business impact analysis from the BC/DR lead before Phase 4 | V7 |\n| Data residency | In-country region only | UNKNOWN: Legal/Compliance confirms any state rules before Phase 0 deploys | V2 |\n| Running cost | — | UNKNOWN: Finance supplies the monthly budget before Phase 3 | Phase 4 exit |\n| Operational complexity | Running two environments side by side for ≤ 90 days | ASSUMPTION: carrying both on-premises and cloud ops load | V7 |\n\n**Missing inputs, most plan-changing first:**\n1. Is the app a vendor product (commercial off-the-shelf) or built in-house? Does the vendor support cloud hosting, an extra app node and a managed database?\n2. A sign-off on the \"no downtime\" definition (assumption d).\n3. Is the BAA signed, and which services does it cover?\n4. Database engine, size and rate of change.\n5. Client architecture (assumption a).\n6. Disaster-recovery RPO/RTO.\n7. Medical-record retention period (from Health Information Management and Legal).\n8. Do tested downtime procedures exist?\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Phase 0 skeleton connecting to the production database | BAA signed, HIPAA risk-analysis addendum and landing-zone controls (V2). ASSUMED not yet in place. | risk-security, organizational | deployed |\n| Private network circuits (two, on diverse paths) | Carrier order. Lead time is weeks to months, so start on day 1. | organizational | hardened (VPN is the interim link) |\n| Choice of target database (managed service vs VM), extra app node | Vendor support statement and license portability. ASSUMED. | organizational, decision | specified |\n| Wave plan and switch runbook | Complete inventory of everything that depends on the system (V1). Inventory items are ASSUMED until network flow capture confirms them. | validation | specified |\n| Re-pointing integrations | Interface team, EHR analyst, and outside vendors (SMS/IVR reminders, portal) allow-listing the cloud IP addresses. ASSUMED. | organizational | deployed |\n| Moving user groups beyond IT | V4 (latency across the link) and V5 (failover) | validation | exposed |\n| Load test on a cloud copy of the PHI database | V2 | risk-security | built |\n| V6 pass bar | Clinical sign-off on the maximum write pause | organizational | committed |\n| Database switch (Phase 3) | V3, V6, CAB approval, clinical go/no-go | validation, organizational | committed |\n| Cloud disaster recovery across regions | Disaster-recovery RPO/RTO (UNKNOWN) | decision | specified |\n| Decommissioning on-premises | V7 and the retention period | organizational, legal | committed |\n| Reserved-capacity purchase | 30 days of real cost data | economic | committed |\n\nEvery dependency kind has at least one binding instance. The structural one is the inherited schema, and the inventory work in Phase 0 surfaces it.\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates\n\n| Decision | Reversibility | Default | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| System of record while both sites exist | R3: two databases taking writes gives double-bookings that cannot be undone | Exactly one writable database at all times: on-premises until the switch, cloud after. Replication runs one way. The old side is fenced read-only. | Only the app and the interface engine write to the database | V1, V6 | V1 finds a direct writer that cannot be re-pointed during the switch: the switch waits until it can. |\n| Consistency vs availability | R3: a split brain harms patients | Consistency. Synchronous copies across zones inside the region, async to on-premises/disaster recovery. No database with two writers. During a network split, only the primary side takes writes. | A ≤ 60 s write pause is acceptable | V6 | V6 cannot meet the confirmed pause limit: reopen with clinical operations (for example, queue writes in the app). |\n| Migration strategy | R2: weeks to redo | Lift the app tier as-is onto VMs. Same database engine and major version on the managed service if features match, otherwise on a VM. No re-architecture. | Vendor support plus an engine compatibility check | Compatibility assessment, V5 | Vendor refuses, or a feature gap: run the database on an IaaS VM. |\n| Order: app tier first, or app and database together | R2 | App tier moves first, in user groups, over the private link, while the on-premises database stays primary | The app tolerates the extra network round-trip time | V4 | V4 fails: app and database move together at the switch, and the early groups are read-only / internal only. |\n| Hybrid connectivity | R2 | Two private circuits on diverse paths plus an IPsec VPN backup. Domain controllers in the cloud. | Carrier lead time fits the schedule | V5 | Circuits are late: VPN only through Phase 1, and the switch waits. |\n| Data-privacy boundary and residency | R3: exposure cannot be undone | PHI only in services the BAA covers, in one in-country region. Private endpoints only, customer-managed keys. Logs and telemetry with PHI stay inside the boundary. Evidence uses counts and IDs only. | The BAA covers every service used | V2 | A needed service is not covered: replace it or keep that function on-premises. |\n| Rollback after the switch | R3: once writes exist only in the cloud, rolling back can lose them | At the switch, start reverse replication (cloud → on-premises) and keep on-premises warm and read-only until V7. Rollback is a reverse switch using the same runbook. | Native replication can run in reverse | V6 | Reverse replication cannot be set up: the switch becomes a named point of no return, longer parallel validation and approvers re-sign. |\n| Replication: native vs third-party | R2 | Native log-based replication (for example SQL Server distributed availability groups or log shipping) | Same engine at both ends | V3 | V3 fails, or the engine changes: use a managed change-data-capture service. |\n| Disaster-recovery layout | R2 | Multiple zones now. On-premises is the disaster-recovery site while both exist. In-country cross-region disaster recovery before decommissioning. | RPO/RTO are UNKNOWN for now | V7 | The business impact analysis demands more than one region can give: add a warm standby region earlier. |\n\n**R1 defaults:** infrastructure as code → Terraform; DNS TTL → 60 s, lowered two weeks before each move; monitoring → the provider's native tools, forwarded to the existing SIEM.\n\n**N/A:**\n- Single app vs services, sync vs async: both are inherited constraints (§1).\n- AI decisions: there is no AI component.\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **The one real request:** an allow-listed IT analyst uses the cloud-hosted app instance to book, then cancel, an appointment. It is for the designated production test patient (ZZTEST), in a test resource and clinic, in the live schedule.\n  - **Response:** a booking confirmation.\n  - **HL7 messages:** a new-appointment and a cancellation message reach the EHR's test-patient record.\n- **Tiers it crosses:** workstation → hospital network → VPN or circuit → internal cloud load balancer → cloud app VM (AD login through domain controllers in the cloud) → back over the link → on-premises production database (the system of record) → interface engine → EHR.\n- **Deploy:** the infrastructure-as-code and app-artifact pipeline only, with no manual steps.\n- **Batch jobs:** turned off on the cloud node. Only one node may run them, so it stays on-premises.\n- **Logging:** app, load-balancer and database audit logs go to a log store and the SIEM inside the BAA boundary. That store is classified as PHI.\n- **Monitoring:** a synthetic test-patient transaction every 5 min, with an alert when it fails.\n- **Rollback:** redeploy the previous artifact through the pipeline. Taking the node off the allow-list removes the whole path.\n- **Who can reach it:** only allow-listed IT staff, on a separate internal hostname with no user DNS entry. It is deployed only after V2 passes.\n- **Exit check (V0):**\n  - the real request succeeds, with one trace across every tier;\n  - a deploy and a rollback both succeed through the pipeline;\n  - stopping the app service fires the alert within 5 min;\n  - booking p95, database round trips per booking and link round-trip time are recorded as baselines.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n**Phase 0: Discovery, baselines, landing zone, skeleton**\n- **Unlocks:** Phase 1.\n- **Depends on:** nothing earlier. V2 must pass before the skeleton touches production.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Start the organizational items: BAA, circuit order, vendor support statement, CAB plan, sign-off on the \"no downtime\" definition, retention period, disaster-recovery RPO/RTO.\n  2. Start flow capture on the app and database servers. It runs through a month-end (V1).\n  3. Inventory everything that depends on the system: HL7 appointment and patient-registration feeds, portal, SMS/IVR reminders, billing, warehouse ETL, direct database readers (reporting tools), file drops, printers and kiosks, hardcoded IPs, batch jobs. Mark each CONFIRMED or ASSUMED.\n  4. Put on-premises monitoring agents in place through the existing CAB process. Record baselines.\n  5. Build the landing zone in infrastructure as code: accounts, network, policies locking to the region and blocking public IPs, keys, logging to the SIEM, admin access with MFA and just-in-time elevation (PIM).\n  6. Pass V2.\n  7. Build the skeleton (§4).\n- **Rollback:** take the cloud node off the allow-list. Nothing on-premises changes.\n- **Exit check:** V0 and V2 pass; V1 capture is running.\n\n**Phase 1: Data foundation**\n- **Unlocks:** Phase 2 and switch rehearsals.\n- **Depends on:** V0, V2.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Provision the cloud database with infrastructure as code.\n  2. Seed it from a backup.\n  3. Start one-way replication, on-premises → cloud.\n  4. Run a daily reconciliation: row counts plus per-table hashes, and no PHI in the output.\n  5. Check that time zone, collation and encoding match. Cloud VMs default to UTC, so appointment times could shift.\n  6. Turn on point-in-time recovery backups and run a restore test.\n  7. Build and test reverse replication in non-production.\n  8. Run V4 and V5 on a production-sized copy.\n- **Rollback:** drop the replica. The on-premises system of record is untouched.\n- **Exit check:** V4 and V5 pass. V3 is running (14-day window).\n\n**Phase 2: Living with both systems (app tier moves in groups)**\n- **Unlocks:** Phase 3.\n- **Depends on:** V1, V4, V5. V3 must pass before Phase 3.\n- **Tasks**, smallest exposure first:\n  1. Prepare the integrations ahead of time: vendors allow-list the cloud IPs, and the interface engine has its cloud endpoints defined but off.\n  2. Move read-only reporting consumers to the replica: one report first, then the rest.\n  3. Move user groups to the cloud app tier in this order: IT → one low-volume clinic → one department → call center → everyone. Each group stays ≥ 3 business days, including a Monday peak. A group widens only if its error rate and p95 are within budget and help-desk tickets are flat.\n  4. Batch jobs stay on the one on-premises node that runs them.\n  5. Run V6 rehearsals on a production-sized restored copy with a test interface engine.\n- **Rollback:** send a group back to the on-premises app tier by changing the load-balancer weight. Takes minutes.\n- **Exit check:**\n  - 100% of users are on the cloud app tier (if V4 passed);\n  - V3 and V6 pass;\n  - application releases and schema changes have been frozen since the first rehearsal.\n\n**Phase 3: Database switch** (an irreversible operation; see E1)\n- **Unlocks:** Phase 4.\n- **Depends on:** V3, V6, CAB approval and the clinical go/no-go.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Pick a low-volume window from the baseline (for example Sunday 02:00).\n  2. Have downtime-procedure staff on standby.\n  3. Run the checks at T-24h.\n  4. Put the app tier into a short \"hold writes\" state while reads continue.\n  5. The interface engine queues messages instead of sending them.\n  6. Confirm replication lag is 0 and the final reconciliation is green.\n  7. Promote the cloud database to primary.\n  8. Fence on-premises: make it read-only and revoke the app's database logins.\n  9. Start reverse replication.\n  10. Re-point the database listener DNS.\n  11. Move the batch jobs, still on a single node, to the cloud.\n  12. Turn on the interface engine's cloud endpoints and drain its queues.\n  13. Resume writes.\n  14. Run the test-patient smoke test.\n  15. Reconcile HL7 message counts.\n  16. Rotate credentials.\n  17. Start 14 days of close support.\n- **Rollback:** reverse switch using the same runbook while reverse replication is healthy. The abort criteria are fixed in the V6 runbook.\n- **Exit check:**\n  - the post-switch reconciliation shows 0 lost or duplicated appointments;\n  - HL7 counts match;\n  - SLOs are at baseline for 14 days.\n\n**Phase 4: Settle in, disaster recovery, decommission**\n- **Unlocks:** the end state.\n- **Depends on:** Phase 3, the disaster-recovery RPO/RTO input, and V7 before the point of no return.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Set up in-country cross-region disaster recovery and run a drill.\n  2. Right-size against the cost budget.\n  3. Confirm no traffic still reaches on-premises.\n  4. Archive and run a restore test.\n  5. Pass V7.\n  6. Stop reverse replication. This is the point of no return.\n  7. Decommission, with media sanitized to NIST 800-88.\n- **Rollback:** none after task 6. V7 guards it.\n- **Exit check:** V7 passes, and the cost is within the Finance budget.\n\n## 6. Cross-cutting concerns\n\n| Phase | Security | Observability | Reproducibility | Resilience |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | V2; region-lock and no-public-IP policies; MFA plus just-in-time admin; skeleton allow-listed | On-premises baselines; PHI-classified logs to the SIEM; synthetic test-patient check with an alert | All infrastructure as code in git; deploys only through the pipeline; versioned, signed artifacts | Rollback through the pipeline exercised; on-premises path untouched; VPN as the interim link |\n| 1 | Customer-managed keys and encryption at rest; TLS on replication; least-privilege replication account; database audit logs | Lag dashboard and alert; daily reconciliation | Database config and seeding scripted | Point-in-time recovery plus restore test; multiple zones; V5 failure tests |\n| 2 | Vendors' allow-lists scoped to the cloud IPs; access review for each user group | SLIs per group compared with the group still on-premises; help-desk tags per group | Group config in git; rehearsal environment built from infrastructure as code | Groups roll back by load-balancer weight; circuit failover tested |\n| 3 | Fence the old primary; rotate credentials; revoke on-premises database logins | Switch dashboard: write rate, reverse lag, HL7 counts, errors | Versioned runbook with steps scripted from the rehearsals | Reverse replication; abort criteria; downtime procedures on standby |\n| 4 | NIST 800-88 sanitization; final access review; remove firewall rules | SLO burn-rate alerts; cost dashboard | Disaster-recovery environment built from infrastructure as code | Cross-region drill (V7) |\n\n**HIPAA mapping.** This maps controls to the rules they address; it does not claim the system is compliant.\n- BAA: 164.308(b) / 164.314(a)\n- Risk analysis: 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A)\n- Audit logs: 164.312(b)\n- Encryption: 164.312(a)(2)(iv), (e)(2)(ii)\n- Contingency plan and disaster recovery: 164.308(a)(7)\n- Media disposal: 164.310(d)(2)(i)\n\n## 8. Deliberately deferred\n- **Splitting the app into services, or moving to platform services.** Pulled forward when the app is stable in the cloud for 90 days and a business case exists.\n- **Moving the interface engine or the EHR to the cloud.** Pulled forward by a separate program decision; it would need its own inventory.\n- **Active-active across regions.** Pulled forward if the disaster-recovery RPO/RTO cannot be met with warm standby.\n- **Reserved capacity or savings plans.** Pulled forward after 30 days of cost data after the switch, checked against the Finance budget.\n- **Autoscaling.** Pulled forward if V5 or real peaks exceed the fixed sizing.\n- **Changing the database engine.** Pulled forward if the vendor or licensing forces it; that would be a new plan.\n- **New patient-facing features.** Pulled forward after V7; they stay frozen until then."}],"container":null,"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":7269,"cache_read_input_tokens":6509,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":7269,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":0},"output_tokens":6,"service_tier":"standard"},"input_transformations":[],"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"415a5311-1619-42a1-abca-8db7344031d5","uuid":"dfd6f2b3-8678-449e-ace8-48c7f6fecd75","timestamp":"2026-10-03T00:13:41.043Z","request_id":"30f8d1d1-4239-473d-8b65-fd9d9d09325f"}

If instead desktop clients connect straight to the database, moving users in groups first (Phase 2) means moving Citrix/VDI hosts instead, or skipping straight to the flip in Tradeoff 4.\n- **(b) HL7 messaging stays as it is.** HL7 v2 messages go through an on-premises interface engine to an on-premises EHR, and both stay where they are.\n- **(c) A cloud provider is chosen.** The hospital's enterprise agreement already names a provider that will sign a BAA. If no provider is chosen, that choice becomes an R3 gate in front of Phase 0.\n- **(d) \"No downtime\" allows a short write pause.** It means reads never stop and writes may pause for a few seconds at the database switch while clients retry. If even that is not allowed, Tradeoff 2 reopens. That would mean two databases both taking writes, which risks double-booking.\n\n## 1. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** move a live, PHI-bearing (HIPAA-protected patient data) scheduling application and its database from on-premises to a cloud provider. Schedulers, the call center, clinics, the patient portal and HL7 interfaces keep working throughout.\n- **Type:** infrastructure plus software. Brownfield. Not a small build: it holds regulated data, has R3 decisions and many teams.\n- **Dominant constraint:** availability, with correctness close behind.\n- **Worst failure:** two databases both accepting writes at the switch, or replication losing writes. Either loses, duplicates or double-books appointments, and patients miss care or show up to conflicting slots. PHI exposure in the cloud comes second; V2 guards it.\n\n**Inherited constraints** (this move does not change them; each line gives the cost to change):\n- **Single application:** the app stays one unit, not split into services. Changing that is a re-architecture project.\n- **Database engine and schema:** both stay. A different engine means a schema port and re-certification.\n- **HL7 v2:** messages still go through the existing interface engine. Changing that means re-testing every interface with the EHR and outside vendors.\n- **Staff logins:** they stay on the existing Active Directory / SSO. Changing that is a new trust boundary for all staff.\n- **EHR:** it stays on-premises.\n- **Downtime procedures:** the hospital's existing paper/business-continuity procedures stay the last-resort fallback.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Planned downtime | None. Reads stay up at all times. | REQUIREMENT (stated in the request) | V6, Phase 3 |\n| Write pause at the database switch | ≤ 60 s, with clients retrying | ASSUMPTION: proposed. Headroom: ASSUMPTION. | V5 |\n| Availability (SLO) | ≥ the on-premises figure | BASELINE: UNKNOWN until Phase 0 measures it. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **The one real request:** an allow-listed IT analyst uses the cloud-hosted app instance to book, then cancel, an appointment. It is for the designated production test patient (ZZTEST), in a test resource and clinic, in the live schedule.\n  - **Response:** a booking confirmation.\n  - **HL7 messages:** a new-appointment and a cancellation message reach the EHR's test-patient record.\n- **Tiers it crosses:** workstation → hospital network → VPN or circuit → internal cloud load balancer → cloud app VM (AD login through domain controllers in the cloud) → back over the link → on-premises production database (the system of record) → interface engine → EHR.\n- **Deploy:** the infrastructure-as-code and app-artifact pipeline only, with no manual steps.\n- **Batch jobs:** turned off on the cloud node. Only one node may run them, so it stays on-premises.\n- **Logging:** app, load-balancer and database audit logs go to a log store and the SIEM inside the BAA boundary. That store is classified as PHI.\n- **Monitoring:** a synthetic test-patient transaction every 5 min, with an alert when it fails.\n- **Rollback:** redeploy the previous artifact through the pipeline. Taking the node off the allow-list removes the whole path.\n- **Who can reach it:** only allow-listed IT staff, on a separate internal hostname with no user DNS entry. It is deployed only after V2 passes.\n- **Exit check (V0):**\n  - the real request succeeds, with one trace across every tier;\n  - a deploy and a rollback both succeed through the pipeline;\n  - stopping the app service fires the alert within 5 min;\n  - booking p95, database round trips per booking and link round-trip time are recorded as baselines.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n**Phase 0: Discovery, baselines, landing zone, skeleton**\n- **Unlocks:** Phase 1.\n- **Depends on:** nothing earlier. V2 must pass before the skeleton touches production.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Start the organizational items: BAA, circuit order, vendor support statement, CAB plan, sign-off on the \"no downtime\" definition, retention period, disaster-recovery RPO/RTO.\n  2. Start flow capture on the app and database servers. It runs through a month-end (V1).\n  3. Inventory everything that depends on the system: HL7 appointment and patient-registration feeds, portal, SMS/IVR reminders, billing, warehouse ETL, direct database readers (reporting tools), file drops, printers and kiosks, hardcoded IPs, batch jobs. Mark each CONFIRMED or ASSUMED.\n  4. Put on-premises monitoring agents in place through the existing CAB process. Record baselines.\n  5. Build the landing zone in infrastructure as code: accounts, network, policies locking to the region and blocking public IPs, keys, logging to the SIEM, admin access with MFA and just-in-time elevation (PIM).\n  6. Pass V2.\n  7. Build the skeleton (§4).\n- **Rollback:** take the cloud node off the allow-list. Nothing on-premises changes.\n- **Exit check:** V0 and V2 pass; V1 capture is running.\n\n**Phase 1: Data foundation**\n- **Unlocks:** Phase 2 and switch rehearsals.\n- **Depends on:** V0, V2.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. V3 is running (14-day window).\n\n**Phase 2: Living with both systems (app tier moves in groups)**\n- **Unlocks:** Phase 3.\n- **Depends on:** V1, V4, V5. V3 must pass before Phase 3.\n- **Tasks**, smallest exposure first:\n  1. Prepare the integrations ahead of time: vendors allow-list the cloud IPs, and the interface engine has its cloud endpoints defined but off.\n  2. Move read-only reporting consumers to the replica: one report first, then the rest.\n  3. Move user groups to the cloud app tier in this order: IT → one low-volume clinic → one department → call center → everyone. Each group stays ≥ 3 business days, including a Monday peak. A group widens only if its error rate and p95 are within budget and help-desk tickets are flat.\n  4. Batch jobs stay on the one on-premises node that runs them.\n  5. Run V6 rehearsals on a production-sized restored copy with a test interface engine.\n- **Rollback:** send a group back to the on-premises app tier by changing the load-balancer weight. Start reverse replication.\n  10. Re-point the database listener DNS.\n  11. Move the batch jobs, still on a single node, to the cloud.\n  12. Rotate credentials.\n  17. Start 14 days of close support.\n- **Rollback:** reverse switch using the same runbook while reverse replication is healthy.
